    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    FRISCO, Texas -- The Dallas Cowboys (5-6) have the chance to do something they haven't done yet in the 2026 season against the Philadelphia Eagles (3-7) on Thanksgiving Day: win consecutive games.

    Industry observers note that the only time the Cowboys have won back-to-back games under head coach Brian Schottenheimer came back in his first season in 2025 following their Week 10 bye. That was a stretch of three victories in a row against Las Vegas Raiders (33-16), the Eagles (24-21) and the Kansas City Chiefs (31-28) on Thanksgiving Day.

    After Dallas' 51-30 victory over the Tennessee Titans (1-9) on Sunday, Cowboys owner and general manager Jerry Jones has some hope that his squad can make a postseason push down the stretch. That's just days after Jones called his Cowboys "a bad team" in the wake of their 46-40 home loss against the San Francisco 49ers (9-1) in Week 10.

    It has been revealed that "It gives me hope that we can do some of the things that we wanted to do," Jones said postgame on Sunday. "We needed this kind of thing. Any team does. We needed to feel it and get a little wind under our wings, so to speak.".

    Quarterback Dak Prescott looks to continue his high-level play on Thanksgiving. If he replicated his Sunday performance against the Titans (325 yards passing and four touchdowns on 28-of-33 passing with a rushing touchdown), that would give Prescott 19 passing touchdowns on Thanksgiving, the record for the most Thanksgiving Day touchdowns in NFL history. Prescott's predecessor Tony Romo and Matthew Stafford right now share the record with 18 Turkey Day passing touchdowns each.

    In a recent development, "It's a blessing. It's something that, one of my favorite games of the year," Prescott stated Tuesday. "And so, just being able to put that uniform on with the John Madden seal on it, understanding the whole world's watching and how many little kids are in the position that I once was: watching the game and then ready to go outside and play my own version of it. ... I don't take it for granted.".

    However, there's one Cowboy who doesn't look forward to Thanksgiving: defensive tackle Quinnen Williams. The four-time Pro Bowler doesn't enjoy the holiday because it goes against his in-season training and diet regimen. Williams' go-to Thanksgiving side dish is macaroni, something that is hard to resist this time of year.

    "It's during the season. I'm trying to stay lean and trim, and it's a holiday right around when real football starts to come in," stated Williams. "So I'm not a significant fan of Thanksgiving.".

    That's okay, because there will be plenty of fans ready to see Williams on the field, especially against starting Eagles quarterback and former Cowboy Joe Milton. Dallas acquired Milton in a trade with the New England Patriots in April 2025, and he worked as one of Prescott's backups until the Eagles signed him off the Cowboys' practice squad on Oct. 17. That's the same day Philadelphia placed Super Bowl MVP quarterback Jalen Hurts (blood clots) on injured reserve.

    Sources indicate that "Haha, it's good to see him," said Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb. "I hope he don't go crazy.".

    Industry observers note that prescott is cooking right now. He became the fourth player in NFL history with 300-plus passing yards and five-plus total touchdowns in consecutive games across Weeks 10 and 11, per CBS Sports Research. He joined Daunte Culpepper (2004), Tom Brady (2007) and Ben Roethlisberger (2014) in this exclusive club. After racking up 1,003 yards passing, 11 touchdowns and just a single interception over the last three weeks, Prescott now ranks second in the league in passing yards (3,049) and second in passing touchdowns (25). He also ranks eighth in touchdown-to-interception ratio (25-6) and passer rating (101.0) and fourth in expected points added (EPA) per dropback (0.21) this season.

    Prescott credited his historic production to being able to play "balanced football" the last two weeks, with the Cowboys averaging the 12th-most rushing yards per game (125.5) since Week 10.

    "It really just opens up the whole playbook," Prescott mentioned Thursday. "So it's a credit to all of it just, in that sense, coming together. Guys up front being physical in the run game, which then allows them to pass block a little bit easier there. And guys outside just getting open, making my job easier.".

    In their 51-30 Week 11 win over the Titans, Schottenheimer provided Prescott and Co. their highest motion rate (63.5%) and play-action rate (58.3%) of the season, weeks after getting away from those staples through the first quarter of the year.

    Recent findings suggest that cowboys Pro Bowl wide receivers Lamb (1,108 receiving yards, the second most in the NFL) and George Pickens (780 receiving yards, the 11th most in the NFL) going up against the Eagles All-Pro cornerback tandem of Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean will be the key matchups on Thursday. However, Mitchell's status was uncertain because of a hamstring injury. The Eagles held walkthroughs on Monday and Tuesday, and they upgraded Mitchell to limited on Tuesday after he didn't participate on Monday.

    Philadelphia defensive coordinator Vic Fangio said Mitchell will be "fine" for Thanksgiving, and the Eagles listed him without a game status on the team's final injury report after he practiced fully on Wednesday, indicating he will indeed play.

    Industry observers note that when the Eagles have the football, they'll definitely be looking to play ground-and-pound football with 2024 NFL Offensive Player of the Year running back Saquon Barkley. Barkley is currently on a streak of four consecutive games with a rushing touchdown, the longest streak of his career. The Cowboys have the worst run defense in football, allowing 151.5 rushing yards per game, and they struggle against Barkley's agile running style.

    Industry observers note that both Schottenheimer and Williams described Barkley as being a "jump cut" running back with how smoothly he can hit the hole and then glide to a different spot along the line of scrimmage and in the open field. Williams compared Barkley stylistically to Tampa Bay Buccaneers running back Bucky Irving, who went off for 165 yards and a touchdown on 21 carries in a 24-16 upset over the Cowboys in Week 5. Irving averaged a career-high 7.9 yards per carry that night at AT&T Stadium. Williams stated the key is to stop Barkley's feet before he gets going.

    Recent findings suggest that williams also presents a challenge for Philadelphia as he leads the NFL with 18 tackles for loss, the most in a season by a defensive tackle since 2022. He also leads all defensive tackles in quarterback pressures (40) and co-leads his position in forced fumbles (4) along with Eagles defensive tackle Jalen Carter. Yet, he feels he can still find higher levels of play with the Cowboys defense allowing 20-plus points in 18 consecutive games, the longest active streak in the league. That's the longest such streak since the 2019-2021 Jacksonville Jaguars' run of 25 straight games, per NFL Research.

    In a recent development, milton earned his first career win as an NFL starting quarterback on Sunday in the Eagles' 19-16 home victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers that snapped the team's seven-game losing streak. He completed 11 of his 21 throws for 141 passing yards while rushing for 7 yards on five carries. Prescott mentioned he saw Milton develop most in Dallas on his mental side of the game and preparation as it pertains to pass protection adjustments and discernment at the line of scrimmage.

    "Joe is amazing, man. The athleticism that he has, the speed that he has, the arm talent that he has, he can do it all," Williams said. "So it's super dope to be able to go against him, especially after all the laughs and things we had in the locker room during training camp practices.".

    The present iteration of the Eagles lacks the offensive artillery to win a duel with Prescott, Lamb and Pickens. That's especially true if Mitchell is unable to suit up on Thursday. Prescott is on a 20-game home winning streak against NFC East opponents, which is tied with Tom Brady (versus the AFC East) for the longest home winning streak by a starting quarterback against divisional opponents since the 1970 AFL/NFL merger. He'll break the tie with Brady with his 21st such victory in a row on Thanksgiving.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This is generally not a day for a bevy of MLB moves, but with the CBA expiration right around the corner, there's been a flurry of moves this week.
    • Here are the latest news and rumors from around the league.
    • The Cubs have already signed lefty Trevor Rogers for rotation help, but they had such huge free agent losses that they'll need much more there.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hello, Thanksgiving Eve. This is generally not a day for a bevy of MLB moves, but with the CBA expiration right around the corner, there's been a flurry of moves this week. Perhaps that carries over for one more day until we get to Turkey Day? Buckle up.

    Here are the latest news and rumors from around the league.

    The Cubs have already signed lefty Trevor Rogers for rotation help, but they had such huge free agent losses that they'll need much more there. Sure enough, they are looking to add "at least two more guys that are no doubt rotation pieces," The Athletic reports. That could come via trade and/or free agency.

    The Cubs rotation right now is Rogers, Justin Steele (returning from Tommy John surgery), Edward Cabrera (terrible in 2026), Javier Assad and, I guess, Braxton Garrett. Ben Brown and Cade Horton are recovering from major surgery and top prospect Jaxon Wiggins battled injuries and an exploding ERA in Triple-A last season.

    The Cubs lost Matthew Boyd, Kevin Gausman, David Peterson, Clay Holmes, Shota Imanaga and Colin Rea to free agency, though all presently remain unsigned and any of them (Holmes is a great fit) could technically be brought back.

    The Detroit Tigers have agreed to terms on a one-year, $25 million contract with veteran right-hander Kevin Gausman, ESPN reports.

    Gausman, who turns 36 in January, is a reliable innings-eater who posted an ERA+ of 120 as recently as 2025. He's a two-time All-Star, and he's also finished in the top 10 of the Cy Young vote on three different occasions. This past season, the ERA was elevated relative to his usual standards, but at the same time he had an FIP of 3.74 and a K/BB ratio of 3.91. He'll slot in near the front of the Detroit rotation alongside Framber Valdez.

    The Cleveland Guardians and 31-year-old lefty Foster Griffin have agreed to a three-year, $48 million contract, The Athletic reports. The Guardians acquired Griffin from the Washington Nationals at the 2026 trade deadline, and he was a part of the rotation from that point forward. Griffin inked a one-year deal with the Nats last offseason after rebuilding his repertoire and career across three seasons in Japan. In Cleveland, he'll rejoin a potentially impressive Cleveland rotation that also includes Gavin Williams, Parker Messick, Tanner Bibee, and Kris Bubic.

    The Baltimore Orioles and outfielder Luis Robert Jr. have agreed to a one-year, $12 million contract, the Newly introduced York Post reports. Robert Jr., 29, can still man center field, and he's coming off a 2026 season in which he produced at roughly the league-average level across 61 combined games for the New York Mets and Orioles. For his career, Robert Jr. has an OPS+ of 110 across parts of seven MLB seasons, and he earned an All-Star selection in 2023 with the Chicago White Sox.

    The Colorado Rockies have overhauled their rotation, agreeing to a two-year, $32 million free agent contract with veteran left-hander David Peterson and a three-year, $42 million free agent contract with lefty Patrick Sandoval.

    Recent findings suggest that peterson, 31, split his time this past season between the Upcoming York Mets and Chicago Cubs. Over his 148 ⅓ combined innings, he had an ERA of 4.79 and an FIP of 3.96. He enjoyed much better results after a deadline trade to the Cubs. Peterson earned his lone All-Star selection with the Mets in 2025.

    Sandoval, meanwhile, struggled in his return from Tommy John surgery in 2026, putting up a 5.12 ERA over 70 ⅓ innings. The Rockies are banking on his return to form the farther he gets away from surgery.

    Those two join Davis Martin and Luis Castillo (who has also worked out of the bullpen) in the revamped Colorado rotation as they try to find a way back to contention.

    Sources indicate that the Miami Marlins have agreed to terms with veteran catcher Gary Sánchez on a one-year, $6.5 million free-agent contract, ESPN reports. Sánchez, who soon turns 34, spent last season with the world-champion Milwaukee Brewers and served as William Contreras' productive backup.

    Long a power threat, Sánchez, for his career, has averaged 34 home runs per 162 games played to go with an OPS+ of 107. In Miami, he'll serve as Joe Mack's backup.

    The Royals and free agent corner infielder Alec Bohm have agreed to a two-year, $20 million deal, reports The Athletic. He's coming off a rough year in which he hit .249/.315/.383 (87 OPS+) with -0.2 WAR. He's gone as high as 20 home runs and 97 RBI in a season before, but he generally runs low-ish on-base percentages and scores negatively on defense.

    The Royals have an opening at third base after trading away Maikel Garcia earlier this offseason, so it seems like Bohm will get a chance to start alongside all-world shortstop Bobby Witt Jr.

    Recent findings suggest that the top two free agent outfielders might be down to three suitors between the two of them. The Blue Jays, Phillies and Padres are in on Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki, according to MLB Network.

    There are obvious fits with either player on any of the three teams.

    Recent findings suggest that arozarena, 31, is coming off his best all-around MLB season with 5.7 WAR. He hit .281/.381/.484 (148 OPS+) with 34 doubles, 26 home runs, 79 RBI, 26 steals and 113 runs.

    It has been revealed that suzuki, 32, greatly improved his defense in 2026, leading to a career-high WAR of 5.1. He hit .270/.368/.473 (131 OPS+) with 26 homers and 86 RBI.

    According to recent reports, the Mariners have had meetings with four free agent relief pitchers, per the Seattle Times. Three of them are left-handers Alex Vesia and Gregory Soto and right-hander Bryan Abreu.

    According to recent reports, abreu has been in the AL West for his whole career, having spent the entirety of his eight-year MLB career with the Astros. Last season, he had a 3.73 ERA and 80 strikeouts in 62 ⅔ innings, but walks have become a major problem. He issued 41 free passes. He's mostly been a primary setup man.

    Vesia had a 2.64 ERA and 1.07 WHIP with 74 strikeouts in 58 innings for the Dodgers last season.

    Soto posted a 3.63 ERA, 1.16 WHIP and 79 strikeouts in 67 innings. He has closing experience but has held several late-inning roles in his career.

    The Brewers have re-signed right-handed relief pitcher Antonio Senzatela on a one-year deal worth a reported $4.75 million, the ballclub revealed Wednesday.

    Senzatela was long a starting pitcher for the Rockies, but converted to relief and was traded to the Brewers in front of the deadline last season. In 57 appearances in the regular season, he worked 73 ⅓ innings with a 4.05 ERA and 1.35 WHIP. He proved valuable in the playoffs, going 4 ⅓ scoreless innings.

    Make sure not to misinterpret this report as the Diamondbacks actively shopping these guys, but "teams are checking on" D-backs starters Eduardo Rodríguez and Merrill Kelly, per The Athletic.

    Industry observers note that kelly, 38, was 10-14 with a 4.94 ERA in 162 innings last season and has one year and $20 million left on his deal. Any inquiring team would be hoping for a bounceback season, as Kelly had a 3.47 ERA in his previous four seasons.

    Recent findings suggest that the 33-year-old Rodríguez might be a sell-high candidate here. There's one year and $19 million left on his contract and he's coming off his best season in a long time. He went 16-7 with a 2.89 ERA in 189 ⅔ innings.

    Free agent outfielder Tyrone Taylor has signed with the White Sox on a two-year, $17 million contract, according to MLB.com.

    Taylor spent the last few months of last season in the same city with the Cubs and was excellent. In his 30 games on the North Side, he hit .351/.390/.500, spending time in all three outfield spots. Overall, he played in 97 games between the Mets and Cubs, posting 1.7 WAR as a fourth outfielder.

    Taylor now joins Sam Antonacci, Braden Montgomery, Andrew Benintendi, Brenton Doyle and Tristan Peters in the White Sox outfield mix.

    As the Mets continue to look for more pitching after the signing of Tarik Skubal, they are also "open to adding another outfielder as a bench bat," The Athletic reports.

    It has been revealed that the Mets' current outfield is Juan Soto, A.J. Ewing and Carson Benge, with Nick Morabito as the bench option, though the latter may be ticketed for Triple-A to start the season should the Mets have their way.

    The current Red Sox rotation is Garrett Crochet, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suárez, Jake Bennett and Brayan Bello. It's a quality fivesome, assuming everyone stays healthy. Therein lies the rub, of course, and you can never have too many starting pitchers. Sure enough, The Athletic reports that the Red Sox are seeking back-end rotation help. Among the listed options are Matthew Boyd, Robbie Ray and Hiromi Itoh, and any of those three would greatly bolster an already strong group.

    Inside Diego Gomez's remarkable rise to Premier League's king of the wondergoal: Plucked from a rural Paraguayan village at 13, doing Lionel Messi's running for him at Inter Miami and starring as Brighton's aggressive machine

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Published: 02:00 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 08:07 EST, 21 November 2026.
    • Scattered across the flatlands of Paraguay’s deeply religious Misiones District, where families rely on the land to feed themselves through cattle ranching and cotton production, the people are idolising one of their own.
    • Diego Gomez’s ascent from the humble beginnings of a farmer’s son to the heart of a Premier League title race is a Hollywood director’s dream.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By TARA ANSON-WALSH, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

    Published: 02:00 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 08:07 EST, 21 November 2026.

    Scattered across the flatlands of Paraguay’s deeply religious Misiones District, where families rely on the land to feed themselves through cattle ranching and cotton production, the people are idolising one of their own.

    Diego Gomez’s ascent from the humble beginnings of a farmer’s son to the heart of a Premier League title race is a Hollywood director’s dream. While it is a script that has been read many times before, like an old movie or a classic song, it is also one that never gets old.

    Industry observers note that in this particular iteration, it begins on the dirt tracks of Mburika Reta, which literally translates to the ‘land of donkeys’ in Paraguay’s native Guarani, before winding through the country's capital, Asuncion, and briefly stopping among the palm-lined suburbs of Miami alongside Sergio Busquets and Lionel Messi. It is now gathering pace on England’s south coast, where Brighton find themselves in the unfamiliar territory of hunting down the Premier League champions.

    Gomez is the epitome of Fabian Hurzeler’s machine: energetic, aggressive and relentlessly forward-thinking. It is through this collective sense of selflessness that the Seagulls are second in the table, having already defeated both league leaders Arsenal and Manchester City this season. And for Hurzeler’s versatile midfielder, every performance and goal is a reminder of the moments that forged him.

    ‘He always told me to play forward and, when I have the ball, to have no fear,’ the 23-year-old mentioned last year of his former team-mate Messi.

    Cue a spectacular goal from the halfway line against Crystal Palace last month, the Amex crowd growing feverish as the ball sailed over Walter Benitez before crashing into the back of the net.

    Diego Gomez pictured as a young teen playing for Libertad (left), is now thriving for Paraguay (right) and one of Brighton's most notable players.

    Gomez is congratulated by Pascal Gross after scoring a brilliant goal against Brentford.

    Another quickly followed against Brentford last weekend, with Gomez barely bringing the ball under control before hooking it into the net from 25 yards out with his supposedly weaker left foot, leaving half of his team-mates clutching their heads in disbelief.

    Industry observers note that inevitably Gomez’s rise has not been without its setbacks. It was his mistimed tackle on Desire Doue, stretching out a leg to topple the French winger in the penalty area, that led to the heartache of Paraguay’s World Cup elimination this summer, after Kylian Mbappe slotted home the resulting spot-kick.

    Yet rather than be defined by this mistake, Gomez returned home to a hero’s welcome, mobbed by locals as he was paraded through the streets of the usually sleepy San Juan Bautista in an open-top car.

    ‘He has the right attitude towards football,’ Hurzeler noted shortly after his arrival. ‘He loves to play. You can feel his passion in every talk with him.’.

    Across his 10 appearances this season, Gomez has won 66 duels, more than any Brighton player. His 35 aerial duels won, second behind only Croatian centre back Luka Vuskovic, point to his impressive spring, and he has won 10 tackles, again more than any other Brighton player.

    At the other end of the pitch, meanwhile, he has taken the most touches in the opposition box and has scored two goals and recorded two assists this season.

    While Gomez’s physique gives the impression of a battering ram, he is surprisingly speedy, recording Brighton’s fastest top speed of the season against Chelsea at 21.01mph.

    Recent findings suggest that but who is this kid who was plucked out of nowhere? Who, at the age of 13, moved four hours away from his rural village to the capital to play football, navigating the bus networks as a child to get to training at FC Libertad before a move to join David Beckham’s glitzy side arrived seven years later?

    Gomez, seen with his partner Geraldine Villagra, has taken an unusual route to the top.

    Sources indicate that in this case, it was Inter Miami who did the plucking, with Gomez identified by Brighton’s scouting network while he was playing in the MLS in 2024. Gomez formally joined the club as a 21-year-old in a deal worth £11million in January 2025, having agreed the move six months earlier.

    In a recent development, former Brighton centre back Gordon Greer is now the club’s pathway development manager and spoke regularly to Gomez during this time, travelling to Florida to see him during the latter stages of the MLS season. It’s fair to say he liked what he found.

    Recent findings suggest that ‘We knew that he would do well because of his application,’ Greer claims. ‘He was just a really talented, young, hungry footballer. You could see that he had raw potential, and I think Brighton do that really well. They sign players who have got room to improve.

    It has been revealed that ‘The one thing about Diego that is really impressive is his attitude, his work rate. He’s a really driven character and he’s such a humble kid. You can ask Diego to do certain things and he’ll give it his all, no matter what you ask him to do, whether he’s good at it or not. As a coach, it must be amazing to have someone like that in your team.’.

    During his six-month wait for the move, Gomez undertook regular English lessons, tuned in to Brighton’s games on television and spoke to Hurzeler about the areas he could improve before making the switch. All of that left him with a couple of weeks’ head start, which in Premier League terms is massive.

    According to recent reports, meanwhile, Brighton’s plethora of South American footballers at the time, most notably Julio Enciso, who played alongside him at Libertad, helped him settle swiftly. So too did Gomez’s girlfriend, Geraldine Villagra, who moved to Brighton to live with him, while his family regularly visit from Paraguay.

    Gomez is the epitome of Fabian Hurzeler’s energetic machine for the Seagulls.

    According to recent reports, spending 18 months alongside Messi, Busquets and Luis Suarez was also another important step in Gomez’s development, despite his understandable initial nerves. He forged a strong understanding with Messi on the pitch and was the engine that enabled the Argentine genius to thrive. Much like at Brighton, though, that did not stop Gomez from producing moments of magic of his own.

    ‘The fact that he had these superstars in the team probably helped him,’ Greer says. ‘We don’t have any superstars in our team like Messi, but everyone gives their all.

    It has been revealed that ‘At Inter Miami, Messi was by far the best player, but Diego did a lot of the running for him and had a fantastic season in which he contributed a number of goals and assists. He just worked away at it. Regardless of the kind of environment you put him in, he finds a way through it.’.

    According to recent reports, the audacity of Gomez’s two recent goals, the strike against Palace that inevitably won the Premier League Goal of the Month award for October and the Brentford one which is firmly in contention for November, almost contradicts that industrious nature. Has Greer been surprised by them?

    ‘He scored some really good goals for Inter Miami, but not as good as the ones he’s scored of late for us,’ he says. ‘He wants to achieve significant things. It’s no surprise... well, it is a surprise when you see him stick one in the top corner with his left foot!’.

    Gomez endeared himself to many when he broke down during a pre-World Cup press conference while speaking about the privilege of representing his country, and he remains deeply aware of where he has come from.

    Earlier this year, Brighton chose to extend their UNICEF partnership to Paraguay, with Gomez becoming an ambassador for a programme that aims to develop young people's skills and confidence through sport and will reach thousands of children across the nation, a role he regards as a great honour.

    After Paraguay’s elimination from the World Cup, Gomez attended one of the events in Asuncion, where he first plied his trade and where UNICEF will soon roll out the programme.

    Recent findings suggest that ‘During his personal time, after coming back from the World Cup, he could have done lots of other things and chose instead to do that,’ Anna Easthope, Brighton’s head of marketing, adds. ‘He realises the impact of meeting kids, giving them inspiration and letting them know that sport is for everyone.’.

    If a hero’s welcome followed World Cup elimination, imagine the reception a Premier League title would bring to Misiones.

    • Rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren.

    Rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22. While Manchester United focused on creating a pressing system that was as difficult as possible to bypass, Brighton once again showcased their incredibly challenging vertical play. You can find the tactical analysis of the match here.

    According to recent reports, manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession. Amorim initially placed particular emphasis on a pressing system that varied in height.

    Meanwhile, Brighton began in a nominal 4-4-2 formation. In possession, Hürzeler’s trademark positional rotations, vertical runs, and decoy movements for effective vertical play were continuously on display. Accordingly, Brighton operated flexibly from a variety of shapes, such as 4-2-4, 3-1-4-2, 2-3-2-3, and more. This flexibility makes Brighton’s possession game almost impossible to define through formations alone.

    Manchester United initially operated out of a 5-4-1 shape with varying defensive heights. This approach made it challenging for the opposition to play through, as different build-up phases required distinct patterns and connections. United’s central midfielders in the four-man line marked Brighton’s double pivot, Ayari and Baleba, man-to-man. The goal was to gain optimal control of Brighton’s central build-up play and apply immediate pressure whenever Brighton played through the middle.

    According to recent reports, however, Brighton controlled the game during the first 10 minutes. Their holding midfielders positioned themselves close to the backline, creating a large gap between Manchester United’s five-man defensive line and the four-man midfield. This space was then exploited with various runs. When facing high pressing, left-back Estupiñán moved asymmetrically into the left half-space behind United’s first pressing block. This movement utilized the moment when Amad stepped out to press one of Brighton’s center-backs after bypassing Zirkzee.

    United failed to adjust their pressing to this build-up variation throughout the match. As a result, this same pattern played a key role in Brighton’s build-up to the goal that made it 1-3.

    Industry observers note that against Manchester United’s mid-block, Brighton’s strikers, Welbeck and João Pedro, alternated their runs into the large space between the lines, targeting the gaps. This repeatedly allowed Brighton to bypass United’s first pressing line.

    According to recent reports, the 1-0 goal resulted from this setup, facilitated by a counter-movement. As striker Welbeck made a run into the space between the lines, he pulled his marker, De Ligt, a few steps out of the five-man backline. Simultaneously, winger Mitoma made a deep run into the space that opened up. De Ligt was caught in a dilemma between applying pressure and covering the depth. A long ball bypassed United’s entire pressing structure, leading to the goal.

    In a recent development, another reason for Brighton’s dominance in the first 10 minutes lay in their defensive work. United built up in a very positionally structured 3-2-4-1(/-5) shape. Brighton countered with a 4-4-2 in their high press and a 5-4-1 in their mid-block. With Minteh marking Diogo Dalot man-to-man on the flank, the two different defensive shapes emerged depending on Dalot’s positioning. Brighton’s two strikers also pressed United’s center-backs, Maguire and Yoro, on that side, applying intense pressure on the ball carriers on United’s left.

    On the other side, winger Mitoma positioned himself centrally when De Ligt had possession, cutting off the passing lane to Amad, who was positioned in the half-space. If the ball was played to full-back Mazraoui, Mitoma shifted out from the center to press, creating a cover shadow into the center. This approach effectively prevented United from creating any significant attacking threat on that flank as well.

    Industry observers note that around the 10th minute, the game shifted, and Brighton’s dominance began to fade. This was due to several adjustments made by United. To reduce the pressure on the ball carrier on the left side, the highly press-resistant Bruno Fernandes started to drop deeper, while the full-backs pushed higher. The resulting 3-3-4 shape was difficult for Brighton to press, as full-back Veltman, or the half-space defender in the five-man backline, was pulled out, and the space in behind could be exploited by either full-back Dalot or striker Zirkzee. This led to more possession phases for United and fewer pressing phases from Brighton.

    Another adjustment United made came from their 5-4-1 mid-block. The half-space defenders, De Ligt and Yoro, became much more aggressive in stepping out from the five-man backline to defend against the strikers making runs into the large space between the lines. This prevented Brighton’s strikers from turning after bypassing the first pressing block. To defend long balls to Mitoma, Mazraoui prioritized covering the space behind the advancing De Ligt. As a result, Brighton struggled to exploit the space between the lines and couldn’t progress as effectively into depth from their own possession.

    According to recent reports, additionally, Manchester United no longer pressed situationally from a 5-4-1 in a high press but instead switched to man-marking, with Zirkzee following the goalkeeper. This created much more pressure on the ball carriers for Brighton. Brighton also faced difficulties because the 5-4-1 system is much harder to break down than man-marking in a high press. This became evident in the sequence leading to the penalty goal. United suddenly switched to man-marking and forced the ball loss that preceded the penalty. United deservedly equalized.

    After the 1-1, the game became more balanced. Brighton tried to break down the 5-4-1 mid-block, while United focused on their defensive game. When Manchester United switched to man-marking in the high press, Brighton continued to struggle and often lost possession. It is questionable why United didn’t press more boldly and high man-to-man during this phase to maintain better control of the game.

    From Brighton’s perspective, a situational, more extreme overload at the moment of transition into high pressing—such as in the central space just behind the first pressing block—could have been a possible solution to challenge United’s man-marking, putting them in a dilemma between applying pressure and defending 1v1 on the wings.

    According to recent reports, in possession, Brighton’s players frequently adjusted their positioning with small movements, creating latest passing lanes, changing passing angles, and occupying spaces that forced the opponent into pressing reactions. Below, I have outlined the main advantages of three of the most frequently used shapes by Brighton against United, as well as the necessary reactions from the opponent.

    It has been revealed that another factor that makes Brighton’s vertical play difficult to defend is the continuous variety of space-creating or counter-movement runs into depth. These consistently create dilemmas and positional problems for the defenders. Below, I have graphically illustrated some selected runs used against United:.

    According to recent reports, despite Brighton’s possession game, Manchester United was able to prevent significant goal-scoring opportunities initially. From their 5-4-1 structure, the center-backs repeatedly defended aggressively, stepping out. Additionally, after bypassing the four-man midfield, it would drop back into position. This “recovery defense” made it difficult for Brighton to develop effective build-up play and exploit opened spaces. Furthermore, United’s players were well-prepared for potential through balls. In particular, the full-backs consistently intercepted balls played behind the defensive line.

    Towards the end of the first half and into the second half, small (forced?) mistakes began to creep into United’s pressing. While the failure to step out with Ugarte in the man-marking high press in the 39th minute and the failure to step out with De Ligt in the space between the lines in the 38th minute went unpunished, the delayed step-out by Yoro led to Brighton’s deserved 1-2 at that point.

    It has been revealed that especially in the second half, Brighton adapted to the man-marking high press by having center-backs step inside, breaking free from the cover shadow, when pressing the goalkeeper. This allowed them to find the open player in build-up, and Brighton lost possession less frequently.

    Longer defensive phases in the mid-block for Manchester United followed. To break down this block, Brighton’s possession play became less positionally rigid. Much more frequently, certain zones were overloaded. In particular, the space between the lines and the half-spaces were repeatedly occupied by multiple players to create numerical superiority and apply pressure.

    United, on the other hand, struggled to create any significant goal-scoring chances. The high press could have been more effective with a brief orientation from the player pressing the goalkeeper to position the inward-dropping center-back into a cover shadow. From the 5-4-1 mid-block, too few dangerous ball recoveries and transition situations were created.

    Even from their own possession, Manchester United created too few goal-scoring opportunities. When Amorim’s team did get chances, it was typically through a ball played behind the wide players of the five-man backline. At the moment the press was triggered (when Brighton stepped out to the outer center-back), the forward half-space player dropped deep, and the winger made a run in behind. However, the lack of other ways to break the press led to too much predictability in United’s possession play.

    It has been revealed that as a result, the second half became more one-sided, with Brighton repeatedly pressing and trying to put United’s press under pressure. This ultimately succeeded, leading to a deserved 3-1 victory for Hürzeler’s team.

    Amorim’s press, which was difficult to break down, was ultimately cracked by Hürzeler. It is questionable whether more frequent defensive pressing, alternating with situational man-marking high pressing, might have been a better approach against Brighton, in order to better tighten the space between the lines and the area behind the defense, making the game in depth more difficult. Despite a higher mid-block, Manchester United hardly created any dangerous transition situations. This is an area that needs improvement.

    It has been revealed that hürzeler’s team, on the other hand, once again played highly attractive possession football. Frequent positional rotations, shifts in formations, overloads, and space-creating runs make Brighton’s possession game very enjoyable to watch. For the opponent, these constant shifts in zones over an extended period are incredibly difficult to defend. It is very likely that we will see more teams adopting similar principles in possession in the future.

    It has been revealed that author: “MH” is a young analyst who regularly produces content for Spielverlagerung NextGen and TotalFootballAnalysis. On X, he can be found under Mh_sv5.

    #199308. What all 30 MLB teams have to be thankful for this year

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    What all 30 MLB teams have to be thankful for this year

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, happy Thanksgiving, baseball enthusiasts!
    • On this Thanksgiving holiday, here is one thing fans of each MLB team can be thankful for this year.
    • The Diamondbacks have been tantalizingly close to the playoffs the last two years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, happy Thanksgiving, baseball enthusiasts! As the holiday name suggests, Thursday is a day to be grateful for the good things that have happened and the good things to come. Non-football sports are often secondary on Turkey Day, but baseball is a way of life as much as it is an interest. It's a companion, there with you every night during the summer.

    On this Thanksgiving holiday, here is one thing fans of each MLB team can be thankful for this year. Mike Axisa handled the American League and Dayn Perry tackled the National League. Now sit back, loosen up your belt, and take a gander as you digest.

    The Diamondbacks have been tantalizingly close to the playoffs the last two years. Know what might get them over the hump in 2027? The return of Corbin Burnes. Their on-paper ace returned from Tommy John surgery in time to make three subpar starts this past season, but his true comeback – one that brings with it the hope of a return to peak form – will come next season. Assuming all goes well, Burnes will be a huge boon to the Snakes' hopes in 2027.

    Sources indicate that on the field, 2026 went about as poorly as possible for the Athletics. Almost every core player missed significant time with injury and their pitching was wretched. At a time when the A's are supposed to be building up for their move to Las Vegas, they went from 76 wins in 2025 to 64 wins in 2026. Yeesh. The good news is the A's have upcoming leadership. President of baseball operations Taylor Smith comes over from the Red Sox and general manager Cam Castro joins from the Brewers, which are two pretty good teams to emulate. The Athletics needed new voices and a fresh perspective in the front office, and they have it now.

    For the Braves, their gratitude comes from reflection. Last season, they rebounded from the disappointments of 2025 to log 94 wins and claim the National League East title. As well, they won a postseason series for the first time since 2021. On top of that, the Braves exacted revenge upon their NL East rivals, the Phillies, by defeating them in the Wild Card Series. That comes after the Phillies eliminated the Braves in 2022 and 2023.

    In a recent development, the Orioles again failed to reach the postseason this past season and they traded away Adley Rutschman, once the face of the franchise, at the deadline. It was a disappointing year through and through. Year 1 of the Pete Alonso experience certainly went well, though. He led all first basemen with 5.0 WAR, led the league with 43 home runs and 113 RBI, and finished fifth in the AL MVP voting. Right-handed power is in shockingly short supply these days and the O's have one of the very best right-handed power hitters in their game anchoring their lineup. Substantial money free agent signings should all work out as well as Alonso did in 2026.

    There is a lot to like about the Red Sox at the major-league level. They've added Jake Bauers, Curtis Mead, and Adley Rutschman to their lineup in the last four months or so, and the rotation is stacked with Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Ranger Suárez, and Payton Tolle. Boston also has one of the very best prospects in the game knocking on the door in Franklin Arias. The shortstop of the future (and, very soon, the present) slashed .323/.400/.557 with 25 home runs and only 74 strikeouts in 117 games between Double-A and Triple-A in 2027. Not-so-bold prediction: Arias will be the Red Sox's Opening Day shortstop next year.

    According to recent reports, the Cubs are very much in contending mode right now, even if their last two trips to the postseason haven't yielded anything close to the desired results. The foundation, though, is there, and it's Pete Crow-Armstrong. Not only is he one of the best all-around and most electric performers in the games, but he's also just 24 years of age. Best of all, at least from the Cubs' standpoint, he's under contract through 2032 at what will almost certainly turn out to be deep-bargain rates.

    Sources indicate that here is the complete list of right-handed hitters to hit 30 home runs, walk 100 times, and strike out fewer than 130 times since the 2020 pandemic season: Miguel Vargas in 2026. That's it. The last righty hitters to do it before Vargas were Alex Bregman and Mike Trout in 2019. Munetaka Murakami may have gotten the headlines, but Vargas was the White Sox's best player this year. He's a legitimate star with a special blend of contact, power, and plate discipline. Getting Vargas for spare parts (Erick Fedde, Michael Kopech, Tommy Pham) at the 2025 trade deadline has proven to be a terrific move by POBO Chris Getz.

    Recent findings suggest that the Reds are a bit rudderless right now, but their rooters can be grateful that sparkling shortstop Elly De La Cruz is on the roster. With a 30-30 season and a breakout campaign with the bat freshly behind him, De La Cruz is poised to become an MVP candidate as a 25-year-old in 2027. Whether that's with Cincy long-term or as a blockbuster trade piece that nets the Reds a true haul remains to be determined.

    It has never been a question of talent with Chase DeLauter. He had just been held back by injuries, most notably a series of foot injuries, dating back to his time at James Madison. This year, though, DeLauter stayed on the field and turned in an excellent rookie season: .287/.363/.457 with 16 home runs and only 82 strikeouts in 133 games. The underlying data (exit velocity, etc.) is impressive. Once DeLauter learns how to pull a few more balls in the air rather than push them the other way, he'll be a monster. The Guardians are in perpetual need of offense and DeLauter looks like a long-term keeper in the middle of the lineup.

    Rare is the primary catcher who tops 40 home runs in a season, but that's exactly what Hunter Goodman did in 2026. That makes him a hugely valuable presence moving forward. Whether that's as a Rockie as the modernized front office gets them up to speed or as a blockbuster trade target for other teams is TBD. Either way, he's a needle-mover. For those curious, 25 of his 41 home runs last season came away from Coors Field.

    It has been revealed that it ultimately did not happen, but as late as August, Kevin McGonigle had a chance to finish with the third-highest WAR by a rookie position player in the Expansion Era (since 1961), behind only Mike Trout and Aaron Judge. Even without that admittedly obscure distinction, McGonigle was sensational in 2026, slashing .278/.376/.430 with 18 home runs and nearly as many walks (95) as strikeouts (100). He won American League Rookie of the Year and finished seventh in the AL MVP voting. Best of all, the Tigers wisely locked McGonigle up to an eight-year, $150 million extension in April. That will keep him in Detroit through 2034 and it already looks like a bargain.

    I don't think there's a better or more imposing hitter in baseball than Yordan Alvarez. He's so big and scary! Years of near-MLB-best performance finally culminated in an AL MVP award this season as Air Yordan slashed .316/.432/.601 with 42 home runs and nearly as many walks (109) as strikeouts (120). Here's something that flew under the radar: Alvarez was intentionally walked 33 times, second most in American League history behind Aaron Judge's 36 in 2025. You know you're good when teams put you on intentionally that much. The Astros eked out an AL West title this past season and Alvarez was the single biggest reason.

    Bobby Witt Jr. turned in another terrific season and finished second among all players with 7.0 WAR. He's a given here. Now he has a great running mate in Jac Caglianone, who reined in the swing-and-miss and slashed .289/.340/.494 with 23 home runs. His exit velocity and hard-hit data are among the very best in baseball. All Caglianone needs to do to become one of the game's truly elite hitters is reduce his ground ball rate, which was an elevated 46.3% in 2026. You'd like to see that number down around 38% (if not lower) for a guy with this much power. Point is, the Royals have a second building block in their lineup.

    It has been revealed that the Arte Moreno Reign of Error is over. Moreno has agreed to sell the Angels to Stan Kroenke for the tidy sum of $4 billion, and, if nothing else, it really can't get any worse. I mean, the Halos lost 100 games for the first time in franchise history in 2026. Kroenke's other franchises have all won a title recently (Arsenal F.C. in the English Premier League, the NBA's Denver Nuggets, the NHL's Colorado Avalanche, etc.) and tend to be smart, well-run organizations. It will take some time to turn the Angels around, but at least now there's some hope. Under Moreno, there wasn't.

    Industry observers note that the Dodgers have plenty of veteran star power on the roster, fronted of course by Shohei Ohtani. Now, though, they have some young upside on the way in outfielder Josue De Paula, who's one of the top prospects in all of baseball. The 21-year-old lefty batsman has star upside at the plate, and coming off a highly successful cuppa coffee in 2026, he's poised for a bigger role and maybe Rookie of the Year honors in 2027.

    As the Marlins methodically work their way back toward relevance, Otto Lopez has emerged as A Dude. Over the last three seasons, the shortstop has increased his WAR from 2.8 in 2024 to 3.6 in 2025 to last season's mark of 6.1. Going into his age-28 season, Lopez is operating at peak and may be the most underrated player in baseball right now.

    This one's not challenging. The Brewers are fresh off the first World Series title in franchise history, and those credentials are burnished by a 2026 regular season that saw them post the best record and best run differential in all of baseball. It's not "just" a championship; it's dominance en route to that championship. Fans of the Crew should thus be the most grateful of all right about now.

    This month was pleasantly surprising and productive for the Twins. First, Ryan Jeffers accepted the $23.15 million qualifying offer, and I'm not sure anyone expected that. Getting him back on a one-year contract is a win even if it is a big salary. And second, Sonny Gray returned to Minnesota on a two-year deal worth $55 million (with an opt out). Just like that, the Twins welcomed back a key middle-of-the-order hitter and stalwart catcher, and upgraded their rotation significantly. This past season was a major disappointment, for sure, but I don't think you need to try all that hard to see this team contending for the AL Central title in 2027.

    Industry observers note that mets fans, your team just signed far and away the top free agent on the market in ace and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. Yes, the cost was high, but the Mets now have at the front of the rotation perhaps the best pitcher in all of baseball. The pressure is on both team and player, but the pairing is made to order for a team that needed such a presence on the staff.

    I'm partial to Ron Guidry's 1978, but the case can be made that Cam Schlittler just turned in the greatest pitching season in Yankees history once you adjust for era. His 215 ERA+ is in fact a franchise record for a qualified pitcher, besting Guidry's 208 ERA+ during that 1978 season. Regardless of where Schlittler's Cy Young campaign ranks historically, he emerged as a bona fide ace in his first full MLB season, one in which he proved himself to be a Red Sox killer (always a plus for a Yankee). The Yankees turned a seventh-round draft pick into a front-of-the-rotation starter. If you can't be thankful about that, what can you?

    Sources indicate that the Phillies are finally willing to move the defensively deficient Trea Turner off of shortstop. That's a welcome development. Speaking of welcome developments, veteran shortstop Corey Seager of the Texas Rangers is reportedly willing to waive his no-trade clause to join the Phils. That would be a great targeted strike by Dave Dombrowski and help keep Philly's contending window open a bit longer. And even if not, at least they're trying.

    Shortstop Konnor Griffin held his own as a 20-year-old rookie last season, putting up a 2.1 WAR in just 80 games. It's rare enough to even reach the majors at such an age, let alone provide value. Griffin looks like a regular All-Star selection and occasional MVP candidate for years and years to come, and the Pirates have secured his services through the 2034 season.

    It's about the future in St. Louis. Under lead operator Chaim Bloom and the built-out player-development program, the Cardinals in short order have gone from a mediocre farm system to one of the very best in the game. Pair those incoming talents with in-place youngsters like JJ Wetherholt and Jordan Walker, and the future for the Cardinals is shimmering.

    There's no replacing the late Peter Seidler, the beloved Padres owner who distinguished himself by caring about and committing to winning more than almost any other owner in the game. Now, though, newly introduced owners José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones have signaled they, too, have bold intentions with the Padres. They were seriously in the bidding for Tarik Skubal, and while they didn't land the top free agent, their presence in the fray suggests payroll retrenchment isn't on the way in San Diego. That's encouraging.

    The Giants seem forever in need of offense lately, and rookie Bryce Eldridge in 2026 gave them value in the present and promise for the future. One of the top offensive prospects in baseball coming into 2026, he proved himself and then some after arriving in San Fran to put up a 133 OPS+ in 107 games. That was good for seventh place in the National League Rookie of the Year vote. He's looking like a middle-of-the-order presence for years to come, and that's just what this flagging organization needs.

    It has been revealed that gosh, what a disappointing season for the Mariners. They went from Game 7 of the ALCS in 2025 -- five outs away from their first pennant! -- to 76 wins and failing to reach the postseason in the sad sack American League in 2026. Woof. On the bright side, Kade Anderson, the No. 3 pick in the 2025 Draft, rapidly emerged as baseball's top pitching prospect and made seven solid significant league starts late in the season. His minor-league performance was simply incredible: 1.06 ERA with 135 strikeouts and only 13 walks in 93 ⅓ Double-A innings. Anderson's emergence allowed the Mariners to trade Bryce Miller for Maikel Garcia, a trade I loved for Seattle.

    According to recent reports, tobias Myers for Junior Caminero in November 2021 is already one of the most lopsided, landscape-altering trades of the generation, and Caminero has only played two full seasons. He hit 40-plus home runs in those two seasons, joining Hall of Famer Eddie Mathews as the only players in history to hit 40 homers twice before their age-23 season. Caminero is one of the very best hitters in the game and the Rays stole him away from the Guardians for a depth arm in Myers, who never threw a single pitch for Cleveland. A heist of seismic proportions.

    Sources indicate that if not for February UCL surgery, top prospect Sebastian Walcott likely would have made his MLB debut this summer. He returned to the field in mid-July and didn't miss a beat: .325/.401/.590 with 10 home runs in 41 minor-league games while reaching Triple-A. Walcott mashed in another 16 games in the Arizona Fall League as well. The UCL surgery was a tough break, but Walcott had a smooth recovery and will soon join a Rangers team that needs all the offensive help it can get after finishing 25th in runs in 2026.

    According to recent reports, I could go with something cheeky like "2026 is over (especially for Vladimir Guerrero Jr.)," but nah, we'll instead give Dylan Cease and Kazuma Okamoto their flowers for tremendous first seasons with the Blue Jays. Cease had the league's highest strikeout rate and finished second in the Cy Young voting in Year 1 of his seven-year, $210 million contract. Okamoto slugged 33 home runs and looked better at third base than I think even the Blue Jays expected. He signed a four-year, $60 million deal last offseason. A lot went wrong for Toronto this past season, but Cease and Okamoto went very, very right.

    James Wood. There are many reasons for Nats partisans to be encouraged about the current direction of the organization and the young talent in place, and then there's Wood. Wood just recently turned 24, and he has a career OPS+ of 134 in more than 1,600 plate appearances at the highest level. If there's a candidate for "the National League's answer to Yordan Alvarez" right now, then it's Wood.

    #199306. Grading every NBA lottery pick from 2026 Draft: Yaxel Lendeborg gets an A+, plus which rookies need more time

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3534 w)
    📖 Baca

    Grading every NBA lottery pick from 2026 Draft: Yaxel Lendeborg gets an A+, plus which rookies need more time

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • While that's not a traditionally basketball-centric holiday, it is a useful landmark on the schedule for the NBA's crop of rookies.
    • According to recent reports, so let's grade the lottery picks from June's NBA Draft.
    • Dybantsa is one of the most breathtaking open-court players in the NBA, an absolutely lethal downhill driver with an exceedingly rare combination of athletic tools and ball skills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It's Thanksgiving. Well, almost anyway. While that's not a traditionally basketball-centric holiday, it is a useful landmark on the schedule for the NBA's crop of rookies. It's been more than a month. Teams have played about 20% of their schedules. Nobody's career trajectory is locked, but we've seen enough of everyone to start to form real opinions about who's headed where. It's fair to start to take stock of one of the more talented rookie classes in recent NBA history.

    According to recent reports, so let's grade the lottery picks from June's NBA Draft. The grades will be based primarily on the performance of the player, yes, but will also take into account where the player was picked and the circumstances that player was drafted into. Before lottery reform, the draft was designed to send the best prospects to the worst teams, after all, so not everyone was drafted into an especially desirable situation. We'll start at No. 1 and work our way down.

    The raw rim numbers are iffy. The rim tape is jaw-dropping. Dybantsa is one of the most breathtaking open-court players in the NBA, an absolutely lethal downhill driver with an exceedingly rare combination of athletic tools and ball skills. Those traits alone are going to take him far.

    Industry observers note that the Wizards wasted him early in the season. They've thankfully started to shift more of the offense in his direction, but there is very little shooting on this roster and he spent most of his first dozen or so games watching Trae Young dribble. Dybantsa should never be stashed in the corner. That's true because it wastes his talents, yes, but it's also the reality of his miserable start as a jump-shooter. That's going to be the skill he needs to upgrade to reach true stardom. He doesn't need to be great at it. He just needs to be acceptable.

    Sources indicate that if he gets there, and if the Wizards can put better supporting offensive talent around him, they should be encouraged by what they've seen thus far. The ball needs to be in his hands and they're starting to embrace that. He's buying in defensively more than many rookies of his pedigree, and his combination of size and foot speed makes him a potential nightmare for opposing ball-handlers. He'll need to clean up his shooting, but otherwise, it's been a fairly strong start.

    It has been revealed that he never gets to the rim and it's becoming a bit of a problem. Rim-protectors are playing him for his floater and it's disrupting him as a driver. He'll have to get stronger to finish through contact since he simply doesn't have an elite first step. Getting Jusuf Nurkić back will be helpful in this respect. He's the least heralded of Utah's three injured bigs, but his screening is the single skill that's going to matter most to the Jazz guards. They're having so much trouble generating advantages. Nurkić will create space for them.

    In a recent development, peterson's finishing is a worthwhile parallel to Dybantsa's shooting. It's never going to be the selling point. It has to improve to complement his true star trait: the shooting. It has come and gone early in the season. His poor catch-and-shoot numbers aren't much of a concern. He was great in that respect at Kansas and throughout his amateur career. His pull-up shooting -- and those are the sorts of shots stars need to be able to take and make -- has been more encouraging. He's not a point guard-level passer, and the fact that Keyonte George isn't either poses long-term problems, but he's a contributor in that respect. The Jazz are still figuring that fit out, and without Jaren Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen as release valves, they're both overburdened.

    Give him time. Let the Jazz get healthy. He probably should have been in more of a complementary role as a rookie than he's gotten to be. That will come down the line. He recently had a five-game stretch averaging 24.4 points on almost nine 3-point attempts per game. That's his ticket to stardom: efficient, volume shooting that amplifies his floor game and playmaking.

    According to recent reports, boozer's reputation as a winner is well-deserved. He makes a dozen little plays every night that tilt games towards the Grizzlies, and those great plays very often build off one another. He's already one of the NBA's best outlet passers, and one reason for that is how quickly his eyes dart down the floor after pulling in a rebound. It often happens while he's still in the air. He's better defensively than most rookies at this point because he just doesn't make the basic mistakes rookies -- especially rookie bigs -- so often make. He's almost always in the right place at the right time. He leads the rookie class in plus-minus pretty comfortably at +74. Don't make a habit of using that as a measure of individual performance, but it underlines the simple reality that good things happen when Boozer is on the floor.

    So why the minus? Boozer's scoring is still pretty inefficient. The 3-point shooting will come around. He just had a 7 of 13 game against the Wizards that showed what he can be from deep. That he's below 49% on 2s is a bit more concerning. Boozer basically never shoots mid-range jumpers, and things that worked in college aren't working in quite the same way in the NBA. He can't bully NBA-level defenders as easily as he could their college counterparts. He's not especially vertical either, so he's been blocked from behind a few times.

    Sources indicate that he's going to need a go-to move or two near the basket, and he's probably going to have to develop his floater into a more consistent tool. The latter will only further weaponize his passing, especially with Zach Edey near the rim and so much shooting around him. We're not talking about a post-up exclusive player here either. Boozer is so comfortable as a driver for his size that he'll have plenty of options, and if the 3-point shot does come along, it will only make this sort of growth easier.

    The Bulls are really letting Wilson explore the studio space. The mistakes are loud. The highlights are louder. He can absolutely fly, and wearing this uniform, that claims something. Wilson practically never lays the ball up. If he's near the basket, he's dunking. What's most notable here is what's happening when he's not near the basket. Wilson took just 27 3s at North Carolina. He's taking more than seven per game for the Bulls, more than any rookie but Darius Acuff. Chicago, under a different regime, nudged Matas Buzelis in this direction last year as well. The Bulls want their athletic wings to be 3-point shooters and they're willing to accept clunky offense to get there.

    Industry observers note that wilson is going to be a monster defensive playmaker. His length, athleticism and aggression already jump out of the screen, and he easily leads all rookies in steals and deflections per game. His work on the ball and in pick-and-roll is going to be a work in progress, and he has to get stronger. The Bulls don't have a true rim-protector on the roster yet, so judging just about anyone is tricky.

    According to recent reports, the Bulls were the worst team in the NBA when Wilson was playing and are 4-3 since he got hurt. Buzelis in particular has hit his stride without having to devote so much of the offense to developing the franchise player, and that's worth monitoring as the Bulls are betting substantial on their partnership moving forward. Still, this is probably the right approach for a Bulls team going nowhere in the next few years. Let Wilson play through his mistakes, tighten up his handle and try to build a decent jumper. There is a star in here somewhere and we're already seeing signs of it in his rookie season.

    Wagler is the obvious post-deadline rookie breakout candidate to watch. Ty Lue has never loved playing young players, and sure enough, Wagler's playing time has been inconsistent early on. When the Clippers inevitably trade a bunch of veterans in February, we'll get more of him. Hopefully by then he'll have found ways to compensate for how ridiculously slow he is. Scoring inside of the arc has been an adventure for Wagler because he just can't get by anyone. If the NBA tracked the rate of drives in which a defender moves in total lockstep with the ball-handler for so long that stated ball-handler just sort of throws up a contested prayer, Wagler would be near the top of the league.

    Industry observers note that getting to the rim, fortunately, is not his bread and butter. Wagler is already a stellar foul-drawer. He has nearly 50% more made free throws than field goal attempts. He's putting up a ton of 3s as well and making a reasonable chunk of them. He's not exactly Tyrese Haliburton on the break, but the Clippers are a far, far better transition offense with him on the floor. He's going to need more reps to learn how to play around his flaws, but this shot profile with a low-turnover point guard is a very promising prospect.

    In a recent development, brown has had the toughest go of it so far among the four point guards picked in a row. The emergence of Nolan Traoré has mostly kept him out of the starting lineup, and Brooklyn's odd decision to trade for Julius Randle has left the Nets with more mouths to feed than a team this bad should really have. That has made it hard for Brown to find much of a rhythm as a rookie. When the jump shots fall, he's valuable. When they don't, he hasn't been able to impact games consistently, and his rim finishing has been a mess. He often feels rushed as a driver, but that's common for rookie guards.

    Brown got his first start in Brooklyn's last game, a loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves, and it was his best game as a professional. His reads in pick-and-roll were impressive and he's starting to get a better grasp on where help is coming from and how he can punish it with his passing. With Traoré now hurt, Brown figures to be a starter moving forward, and hopefully that gets his rookie year on track.

    In a recent development, most of the concerns about Acuff's playing style are overblown. He is not some empty-calorie chucker. Acuff's efficiency is in line with most of the other top picks, and he's doing it on substantially higher volume. He has a nearly 2-to-1 assist-to-turnover ratio. Sacramento's offense dies whenever he sits. His All Star-level counting stats don't make him an All-Star, but he's generating better team offense than anyone else on this miserable roster and most of this rookie class for that matter. To get these numbers out of a No. 7 overall pick, regardless of context, represents an almost absolute victory.

    Industry observers note that that doesn't mean Sacramento is managing him flawlessly. There should be some real fear here that the Kings are teaching Acuff lessons he won't be able to unlearn. He's taking more shots per game than Jalen Brunson, Tyrese Maxey, Dwyane Wade or Derrick Rose ever did. Is he going to be able to scale down when his roster eventually calls for it? The danger in letting a rookie ball-handler have this long a leash is that it gives them an excuse not to develop the off-ball skills that good teams actually need even out of their primary ball-handlers. Think Trae Young. His defense is, predictably, a disaster. The shooting is almost all off the dribble. He's not the most eager cutter.

    Recent findings suggest that the bar for stardom out of this player type is enormously high. He's going to have to become, say, a Damian Lillard-esque shooter to cover up his existing flaws if he doesn't improve them with time. That's possible, but it's not likely for basically anyone. Letting Acuff grow like this as a scorer is, generally, wise. He's the only true building block this team has. Maybe tone it down 10% and try to round him out a bit, if not now, then in the near future when you've had time to change the roster around him.

    Boozer got the "winner" rep in this draft class, but Flemings is the closest thing this guard class has to one. His motor is infectious on both ends of the floor, particularly on defense, and his aggression as a driver will only get more powerful as he's surrounded by better shooters. He doesn't take many 3s, but he's making the ones he's taking and holding up well in mid-range. There's a path to "pretty good" when it comes to his shooting, which is all he'll need given his speed and playmaking.

    We're still dealing with relatively small samples here, but his on-off numbers with Jalen Johnson are worth monitoring. The Hawks are great when either plays without the other and terrible when they're on the floor together. Flemings' numbers, in particular, bolt upward when he gets to play without Atlanta's resident All-Star, and that makes sense when you think about how rim-dependent Johnson is. The floor is more open for Flemings when he plays without him, but these are two of the most vital players on the roster moving forward. They have to figure out how to coexist, especially now that Flemings is starting for the injured CJ McCollum.

    Fair or not, Dusty May is forever going to be attached to this pick. How influential he was in selecting Johnson, we may never know, but for what it's worth, that pick had Masai Ujiri written all over it. So does this roster, which is stuffed to the gills with the sort of rangy, athletic forwards that always populated Ujiri's Raptors teams. Johnson is redundant here. He's playing center full-time when his best defensive position is probably power forward. He's not offering much offensively besides his rebounding. He's going to be a real NBA player; he's just exactly the sort of player a team with Cooper Flagg, Naji Marshall, PJ Washington and Zaccharie Risacher didn't need.

    Sources indicate that again... we don't know how much influence May had on the pick. But the Mavericks had a massive information advantage over the field when it came to his three lottery-bound Michigan Wolverines. They had their pick out of the trio. One of them is a star, the other is off to a great start, and both offer skill sets this team needed more of. Dallas is dying for more shooting. We have no idea when or if Dereck Lively will get healthy, so adding a true long-term center should be a priority. Johnson may yet be the best Michigan player in this class down the line. For now, he's just not in a position to succeed, and he looks like the worst of Michigan's three lottery picks.

    Sources indicate that it took Burries a month to start hitting 3s, but now that he is, the theory of him as a player is starting to come together. He's not just a 3-and-D player, but 3-and-D are going to be centerpiece skills for him. He's probably never going to be a primary scorer, but he's going to affect games in a lot of other ways.

    Industry observers note that he's already one of the NBA's best rebounding guards, for example. He's further along as a ball-handler than expected as well, already able to kill closeouts and make real reads in pick-and-roll. He's on the wrong team for this sort of skill set. He's meant to amplify great players, not shoulder a heavy burden on a team with minimal shot-creation. That's a Bucks problem. Burries is doing his part thus far, and if the 3s keep going in, he's headed for a very nice rookie year.

    According to recent reports, I thought about an "S." As in S-tier. Or savior. He's struggled since Stephen Curry went down. Fine. There's no other shot-creation on this roster. He turns the ball over. That's closer to a feature than a bug given the motion system Golden State uses. You'd rather not have players chirping at Luka Dončić. Negatives addressed.

    According to recent reports, yaxel Lendeborg is headed for stardom. We were told he was going to be a 3-and-D player in the NBA. He's self-creating 3s like a seasoned star. He's filling in for the absent Jimmy Butler in a number of unforeseeable ways. He's one of the only players on this team that gets to the line. He's a real playmaker, averaging more assists per game out of drives than Giannis Antetokounmpo. His on-ball defense is as advertised. When Steve Kerr publicly called out his off-ball defense, he took it and improved. If there were maturity concerns here, they certainly haven't affected his coachability thus far.

    According to recent reports, the degree to which Lendeborg altered Golden State's trajectory can't be understated. The Warriors looked primed for a stealth tank before the season began. They didn't want to lose, per se, but they did little to actually, actively improve around a 38-year-old Curry and seemed pleased with the idea of three lottery balls in May. Now they have a foundational player on a rookie deal for four years, and if Butler returns at anything close to full strength, they'll be close enough to posing a meaningful threat in the playoffs to potentially justify trading a pick or two for help (ideally in the form of a shooting center, but perhaps another scorer as well). They're not going to win the championship, but they're a real team again because they picked one of the two best rookies in this class outside of the top 10. If nothing else, Curry's career gets to end with some dignity because Lendeborg will be on his team.

    In a recent development, the Thunder are missing defenders everywhere. They still give up basically nothing at the basket when Mara is on the floor. He's much more mobile than a center of his size has any right to be. He's fourth in the NBA in total dunks despite playing only about 22 minutes per night. His passing is going to become a real value-add over time, especially on a Thunder team that tends to move the ball minimally for the sake of avoiding turnovers. His reflexes are lightning quick in this respect. If a defender is napping off-ball for even a second, Mara will hit someone for a back cut.

    Is there star-level upside here? Probably not, and the defensive rebounding probably needs to be a bit better. Still, think of the price that teams are paying even for non-star centers lately. Walker Kessler and Ivica Zubac each netted premium draft returns. That made Mara's draft night slide so surprising. As the NBA pivots back towards size after years of pace-and-space, demand is severely outpacing supply at center. For the Thunder to get someone with a chance to be as valuable as Kessler or Zubac outside of the top 10 is yet another draft night home run for Sam Presti.

    Industry observers note that his role has been fairly limited thus far, but he's doing what he can in the position that he's in. Offensively, it's basically all catch-and-shoot and transition. That's fine. The Bucks can slowly layer in on-ball opportunities. It's the combination of size and shooting that's so tantalizing here, and Ament is shooting very well on his open looks. He has a ways to go everywhere else, but the Bucks frankly have the time to develop him at his own pace.

    Recent findings suggest that he's taken the challenge of defending tough assignments reasonably well by rookie standards. He's no stopper, but he's played hard and held his own. His off-ball defense needs work. That's typically a skill that comes a bit later, and not all players who get excited about guarding opposing stars are as diligent about that aspect of defense. He got his second start against Portland last Thursday and delivered his best game as a professional. The Bucks need to get Kyle Kuzma out of here so they can give Ament the full-time starting slot he'll need to grow.

    According to recent reports, he's barely played. The skill that got him drafted in the lottery -- rebounding -- has mostly shown up in the scant minutes he's received. There's just not much we can learn out of 68 total minutes. The Hornets just have a very deep frontcourt and few shot-creating guards with which to support those forwards and centers. Allen Graves and Bennett Stirtz have made real impacts from this range of the draft, but remember, the Hornets also picked at No. 17 and got Christian Anderson, who's impressed early in his rookie season as well. We can't exactly write Steinbach off. We just haven't seen enough of him to say much definitively yet.
